periods.activity_title: What Makes a Civilisation? Building the Seven-Characteristic Framework

time_bands.activity: Present the definition of civilisation as an advanced stage of human societies. Ask students: 'What do you think a large group of people living together would need to organise themselves?' Take four or five responses, then introduce the seven characteristics: government and administration, urbanism and town-planning, variety of crafts, internal and external trade, writing, cultural ideas expressed through art or oral traditions, and productive agriculture. Write each characteristic on the board as it is named.

Introduce the term metallurgy — the techniques of extracting, purifying, and combining metals — and add it to the framework on the board as a technology linked to crafts and trade. Then pose the Think About It question from the chapter: 'Which of these seven characteristics is most fundamental — which one makes the others possible?' Give students a quick individual list of reasons for their chosen characteristic, then open a structured whole-class discussion. Push students to explain the dependency: could trade exist without writing? Could cities exist without agriculture?

Students work in pairs. Each pair receives one characteristic (written on a slip of paper or assigned verbally) and constructs a brief argument — two or three sentences — for why their characteristic is the most fundamental. Pairs then share in a rapid round-robin. After all pairs have spoken, the class votes on which argument was most convincing and why.

Bring the discussion to a close by naming the chapter's organising idea: the Sindhu-Sarasvatī civilisation will be examined through each of these seven characteristics across the chapter. Students write one sentence in their notebooks: 'I think [characteristic] is most fundamental because [reason].' This is their personal claim they will test as they learn more.

periods.section_context: Seven characteristics of civilisation, metallurgy definition, Think About It task
periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter's conceptual architecture by establishing the seven-characteristic framework that every subsequent section will test. A common confusion is treating all seven as equally necessary at the same time — students may need to be reminded that civilisations can show these characteristics at different levels of development. Encourage students to hold their 'most fundamental' claim lightly, as later evidence about Harappan agriculture, trade, and writing will give them richer grounds for re-evaluating it.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students study early Indian civilisation as a case of settled urban life, covering agriculture, construction, metallurgy, water technology, craft, trade, and cultural life.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct and defend a criteria-based framework for identifying the features of a complex settled society.

periods.activity_title: From Villages to the First Cities: The Geography of Early Settlement
materials: Printed or projected map showing Punjab, Sindh, Indus River, and Sarasvatī basin
periods.visual_aids: Map of the Indus-Sarasvatī region showing major rivers, Punjab, Sindh, and key Harappan city locations

time_bands.activity: Display or distribute the map of the Indus-Sarasvatī region. Ask students to locate the Indus River and its tributaries and identify the fertile plains of Punjab and Sindh. Introduce the idea that from about 3500 BCE, villages in this region began growing into towns, and by around 2600 BCE the transition to full urbanisation — the 'First Urbanisation of India' — was complete.

Explain the multiple names given to this civilisation — Indus, Harappan, Indus-Sarasvatī, Sindhu-Sarasvatī — and the reason for the name Harappan: the city of Harappa in Pakistan's Punjab was the first site excavated, in 1920–21. Ask students: 'Why might archaeologists name an entire civilisation after the first site they find?' Discuss the idea that naming reflects the order of discovery, not necessarily the most important site. Ask students to suggest what this means for how our knowledge of the civilisation has changed over time.

Run the Let's Explore activity from the chapter: students match major Harappan cities — Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi, Ganweriwala — to their modern states or countries using the map. After matching, ask: 'What does the spread of these cities across modern Pakistan, Gujarat, and Haryana tell us about the size of this civilisation?' Students write a two-sentence inference in their notebooks.

Consolidate by asking students to explain in their own words why the phrase 'First Urbanisation of India' is significant. Take two or three oral responses. Close by noting that the movement from village to city is one of the two great transformations this chapter traces — students will examine the other transformation, the decline, in a later part of the chapter.

periods.section_context: Punjab-Sindh plains, Indus tributaries, 3500–2600 BCE urbanisation, Harappa excavation 1920–21
periods.teacher_notes: This unit traces the geographical and historical roots of the first Indian urbanisation, building on the seven-characteristic framework introduced through the civilisation definition. A common confusion is between the name 'Harappan' (from the excavation site) and the idea that Harappa was necessarily the civilisation's largest or most important city — the matching activity is a good moment to address this. Encourage students to notice that what we call a civilisation depends on which site is found first, which itself is shaped by geography and accident.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students explain major historical changes and their societal impact, including the transformation from villages to planned cities and the later decline.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how geographical conditions drove the transformation from scattered rural settlements to organised urban centres.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students study early Indian civilisation as a case of settled urban life, covering agriculture, construction, metallurgy, water technology, craft, trade, and cultural life.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can connect geographical features — river systems and fertile plains — to the conditions that enabled the emergence of early settled urban life.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students connect natural phenomena and river systems to human settlement patterns and civilisational development.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify the relationship between river geography and the location of early human settlements.

periods.activity_title: The Sarasvatī River: Reading Texts and Maps as Historical Sources
materials: Printed or projected map showing Ghaggar-Hakra course and Harappan sites
Short excerpt from Rig Veda description of the Sarasvatī (teacher-prepared, 2–3 lines)
periods.visual_aids: Map showing the Ghaggar-Hakra river course across India and Pakistan with Harappan site locations plotted along it

time_bands.activity: Display the map showing the Ghaggar-Hakra course and the Harappan sites along it. Ask students to count and name the settlements visible along this river — including Rakhigarhi, Ganweriwala, Farmana, Kalibangan, Bhirrana, and Banawali. Ask: 'What does the density of settlements along this river suggest about its importance?' Take responses, then introduce the river's ancient name: the Sarasvatī, today known as the Ghaggar in India and the Hakra in Pakistan, now flowing only seasonally.

Read aloud the short Rig Veda excerpt describing the Sarasvatī as flowing 'from the mountain to the sea.' Ask: 'What type of source is this? What does it tell us, and what does it not tell us?' Explain that the Rig Veda is an ancient collection of prayers and is a textual source. Compare this with the map, which is an archaeological/geographical source. Ask students: 'Can these two sources together tell us something that neither one could tell us alone?' Guide students to the idea that the text tells us the river was large and revered, while the map shows where settlements clustered — together they indicate the river's role in sustaining civilisation.

Students work individually: draw a simple T-chart in their notebooks labelled 'What the Rig Veda tells us' and 'What the archaeological map tells us.' They complete both columns and then add a third row: 'What we can conclude only by using both sources together.' After completing, two or three students share their third row with the class.

Consolidate by asking: 'Why do historians need more than one type of source?' Take brief responses. Note that later texts describe the Sarasvatī as drying up and disappearing — a fact that will matter when the chapter returns to the question of why the civilisation declined.

periods.section_context: Ghaggar-Hakra course, Sarasvatī in Rig Veda, Rakhigarhi, Kalibangan, Bhirrana, Banawali
periods.teacher_notes: This unit develops the skill of reading a textual source and an archaeological map as complementary — not competing — forms of evidence, using the Sarasvatī River as the content vehicle. A common confusion is treating the Rig Veda as simply a religious text with no historical value; the discussion should help students see that religious texts can preserve geographical and historical memory. The mention of the river drying up is deliberately left as a thread to be picked up in the unit on the civilisation's end.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students interpret multiple source types — textual, archaeological, material — to construct historical understanding.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can compare information from a textual source and an archaeological map to construct an inference neither source supports alone.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students connect natural phenomena and river systems to human settlement patterns and civilisational development.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can use spatial distribution of archaeological sites to reason about a river system's role in supporting human settlement.

periods.activity_title: Planned Cities: Layout, Fortifications, and the Upper and Lower Towns
materials: Projected or printed diagram of a Harappan city layout showing upper and lower town, cardinal-direction streets, and fortifications
periods.visual_aids: Schematic diagram of Harappan city plan with upper town, lower town, cardinal-direction street grid, and fortification walls labelled

time_bands.activity: Display the city layout diagram. Explain that Harappa and Mohenjo-daro in present-day Pakistan were the first two cities of this civilisation identified, in 1924. Point out the cardinal-direction street grid — streets oriented precisely north-south and east-west — and the fortification walls surrounding the city. Ask: 'What does building streets to exact cardinal directions tell us about this society's planning capacity?' Take two or three responses.

Introduce the division into upper town (housing the elite) and lower town (for common people) and the note that both zones used the same quality of brickwork. Ask students: 'Why is it significant that the brickwork quality was the same in both zones?' Discuss the idea that this reveals something about standards and administration. Note large collective structures used for warehousing. Mention that subsequent discoveries — Dholavira in Gujarat, Rakhigarhi in Haryana, Ganweriwala in Pakistan — extended the civilisation well beyond the Indus valley, which is why the term 'Indus Valley civilisation' is now considered obsolete.

Present the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro: a waterproofed tank measuring 12 × 7 metres, surrounded by small rooms and a well. Run the Let's Explore debate from the chapter: was the Great Bath a royal bath or a tank for religious rituals? Divide the class into two groups. Each group prepares two arguments for their assigned interpretation using evidence from the description (waterproofing, surrounding rooms, central location in upper town). Groups present their arguments and the class identifies which evidence supports which interpretation best.

Introduce Dholavira as a unique case: three distinct zones rather than the typical two found in other Harappan cities. Ask: 'What might a third zone suggest about the social structure of Dholavira?' Students write a one-sentence hypothesis in their notebooks. Consolidate: the variety of city layouts across the civilisation shows both shared urban principles and local adaptation.

periods.section_context: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, cardinal streets, upper-lower town division, Great Bath, Dholavira three zones
periods.teacher_notes: This unit develops students' ability to read physical city planning as evidence of administrative sophistication and social organisation, building on the urbanisation process introduced when tracing the growth from villages to cities. A common confusion is assuming the upper town was simply 'better' — students should be guided to notice that the equal brickwork quality complicates a simple hierarchy. The Great Bath debate is genuinely unresolved in scholarship, so both interpretations should be treated as legitimate and evidence-dependent.

competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse physical city planning features as evidence of administrative capacity and social organisation in a settled urban civilisation.

periods.activity_title: Engineering Underground: Drains, Wells, and the Logic of Harappan Water Systems
materials: Projected or printed diagram of Harappan drainage system and well cross-section
Measuring tape or metre rule (for the reservoir comparison activity)
periods.visual_aids: Diagram showing a Harappan home's bathing area connected to the city-wide covered drain network, with a plan of Dholavira's reservoir system

time_bands.activity: Display the drainage diagram. Explain that individual Harappan homes had bathing areas directly connected to a city-wide drainage network running beneath the streets to carry away waste water. Ask students: 'What would need to be planned and coordinated before a single house could be connected to a city-wide drain?' Guide them to recognise that both the house and the drain must be designed together — this requires city-level planning before construction begins.

Describe water supply across different Harappan cities: hundreds of brick-lined wells in Mohenjo-daro; ponds and streams in other regions; and at Dholavira, at least six large reservoirs built with stone or cut into rock, connected by underground drains for water harvesting. The largest Dholavira reservoir measured 73 metres in length. Run the student activity: use a measuring tape to mark out 73 metres in the classroom or corridor (or estimate using the classroom length), and ask students to compare this to familiar spaces in their school.

Pose the Think About It question from the chapter: 'What kind of administrative organisation would be needed to build and maintain the Dholavira reservoir system — six reservoirs, underground drains, and a city-wide water-harvesting network?' Students discuss in groups of three, then each group produces a short written list of the administrative requirements: who decides the design, who organises labour, who maintains the system, who manages access. Groups share their lists and the class compiles a master list on the board.

Bring the activity together by asking: 'Why might different cities — Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, and others — have different water infrastructure?' Guide students to see that geography (availability of rock for cutting, proximity to rivers) shapes the technology chosen. Students write one sentence in their notebooks connecting the Dholavira reservoir system to the chapter's definition of civilisation — specifically its requirement for government and administration.

periods.section_context: Harappan drainage network, Mohenjo-daro wells, Dholavira six reservoirs 73-metre length, administration
periods.teacher_notes: This unit uses water infrastructure as a window into administrative sophistication, extending the city-planning analysis from the town-planning unit by moving from visible layout to buried engineering. A common confusion is treating the drainage system as a modern convenience rather than as evidence of coordinated city-level governance — the group activity on administrative requirements is designed to make this visible. The geographic variation in water technology (wells in Mohenjo-daro, rock-cut reservoirs in Dholavira) helps students see how environment shapes engineering choices.

competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate water management infrastructure as evidence of the administrative and engineering capacity of a complex urban civilisation.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students connect the distribution of resources and geographical conditions to the development of differential infrastructure and technology across sites.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how geographical variation in available resources shaped differential water infrastructure across Harappan cities.

periods.activity_title: Fields, Ploughs, and Pots: Reconstructing Harappan Agriculture and Diet
materials: List of Harappan crops and food items written on board (barley, wheat, millets, rice, pulses, vegetables, cotton, dairy, turmeric, ginger, banana)

time_bands.activity: Ask students: 'How do archaeologists know what people ate thousands of years ago if there is no written menu?' Take responses, then explain the two main sources: animal and fish bones found at excavation sites, and scientific analysis of clay cooking pots that reveal food remains including dairy products, turmeric, ginger, and banana. Write the full list of identified crops and foods on the board: barley, wheat, millets, rice (sometimes), pulses, vegetables, cotton, dairy, turmeric, ginger, banana.

Explain that Harappan settlements were established along rivers both for water and for the fertile riverside soil. Farming tools including ploughs have been found at Banawali in Haryana. Harappans cultivated barley, wheat, millets, sometimes rice, pulses, and various vegetables. Crucially, they were the first in Eurasia to grow cotton, which they wove into clothing. Agricultural activity was managed by numerous small rural villages that supplied the cities. Ask: 'What does the need for small villages supplying cities tell us about how the food system was organised?'

Run the student activity from the chapter: 'Imagine you are preparing a meal using only Harappan ingredients.' Students work individually to write a short description (four to five sentences) of their meal — naming specific ingredients from the board list, explaining how they might have been prepared, and noting one ingredient that surprises them. After writing, three or four students share their meals with the class. The class identifies which ingredients appear in Indian food today and which seem unfamiliar.

Consolidate by asking: 'What does the evidence of cotton cultivation tell us about the Harappan economy beyond just food?' Guide students to see that cotton — the first in Eurasia — links agriculture to craft (weaving) and potentially to trade. Students note this connection in their notebooks as a one-sentence observation.

periods.section_context: Barley, wheat, cotton cultivation, Banawali plough, fish and animal bones, clay pot food analysis
periods.teacher_notes: This unit uses food and agriculture as a lens to demonstrate how archaeologists reconstruct everyday life from physical evidence, extending the source-interpretation skill developed when reading the Sarasvatī River evidence. A common confusion is assuming that 'excavated bones' means the Harappans were primarily hunters — students need to understand that the dominant food base was cultivated grain, with animal protein as a supplement. The cotton cultivation fact is genuinely remarkable and worth dwelling on: it ties agriculture directly to craft and trade.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students study early Indian civilisation as a case of settled urban life, covering agriculture, construction, metallurgy, water technology, craft, trade, and cultural life.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can reconstruct the agricultural and dietary practices of an early civilisation from diverse archaeological evidence including tools, bones, and residue analysis.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students connect the distribution of resources and geographical conditions to the development of differential infrastructure and technology across sites.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can connect river-bank fertile soil and agricultural tool finds to the food-production geography of an early settled civilisation.

periods.activity_title: Carnelian Beads and Shell Bangles: The Craft Foundations of Harappan Trade
materials: Images of carnelian beads and shell bangles (projected or printed)
periods.visual_aids: Projected images of Harappan carnelian beads and shell bangles showing drilling and decorating techniques

time_bands.activity: Display images of carnelian beads and shell bangles. Ask students: 'What would you need to know before you could make and sell these objects?' Take responses, then introduce carnelian as a reddish semiprecious stone found mainly in Gujarat. Explain that Harappan craftspeople developed special drilling and decorating techniques to work with it, making carnelian beads among the most prized trade items of the civilisation. Similarly, shell bangles required sophisticated craftsmanship — conch shells had to be cut, shaped, and smoothed.

Explain the full range of Harappan exports: ornaments, timber, objects of daily use, and probably gold, cotton, and food items. Imports likely included copper. Ask: 'Why is copper an import rather than an export?' Lead students to see that copper ore was not widely available within the civilisation's core territory, so it had to be sourced from outside — this is resource geography shaping trade. Introduce the note that the Harappans mastered copper and bronze metallurgy, using bronze for tools, pots, and figurines, connecting back to the metallurgy definition from the chapter's opening framework.

Students construct a simple trade-flow diagram in their notebooks: two columns labelled 'Exports' and 'Imports,' then a third section labelled 'Raw materials needed for exports' where they identify where key materials came from (carnelian from Gujarat, conch shells from the coast). They then add arrows showing the direction goods moved. After completing the diagram, pairs compare and discuss: 'What does the need to import copper tell us about the geographical limits of this civilisation's own resources?'

Consolidate by asking students to identify the connection between craft specialisation and trade: why do carnelian beads and shell bangles require skilled craftspeople, and how does craft skill become a source of economic value? Students write a one-sentence answer in their notebooks.

periods.section_context: Carnelian beads from Gujarat, shell bangles, exports, copper imports, bronze metallurgy, craft techniques
periods.teacher_notes: This unit examines the craft foundations of Harappan trade, building on the agricultural and raw-material base established when the chapter addressed Harappan food production and cotton cultivation. A common confusion is treating trade as simply 'buying and selling' without recognising the craft labour and geographical sourcing that make trade goods valuable — the diagram activity is designed to make this chain visible. The return to metallurgy here reinforces its importance as a connecting thread across the civilisation's economic life.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students analyse Harappan trade as an economic activity covering commodities, production techniques, routes, and infrastructure.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how craft specialisation and raw material sourcing formed the productive basis of an ancient civilisation's export trade.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students connect the distribution of resources and geographical conditions to the development of differential infrastructure and technology across sites.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace how the geographical distribution of raw materials such as carnelian and copper shaped the commodity structure of Harappan trade.

periods.activity_title: Routes, Rivers, and the Sea: Harappan Trade Networks and the Lothal Dockyard
materials: Map showing Harappan trade routes (overland, river, and maritime) including Lothal's location in Gujarat
periods.visual_aids: Map of Harappan internal and external trade routes showing overland paths, river corridors, and maritime connections, with Lothal marked

time_bands.activity: Display the trade route map. Ask students to trace three different types of route: overland (across land), along rivers, and by sea. Explain that the Harappans conducted trade using all three modes — overland, along rivers, and by sea — and that the chapter describes this as the first intensive maritime activity in India. Ask: 'Why might sea trade be significant in a way that overland trade is not?' Guide students to think about the volume of goods, the distances covered, and the infrastructure required.

Introduce the Lothal dockyard in Gujarat: a large basin measuring 217 × 36 metres. Ask students to visualise this scale — compare the 217-metre length to a known local landmark or two football pitches end to end. Ask: 'What does building a structure of this size tell us about how the Harappans organised the labour and materials required?' Discuss the administrative planning this implies. Note that Lothal's location on the Gujarat coast made it ideally positioned for maritime trade.

Introduce the thousands of small steatite seals bearing animal figures and undeciphered script signs. Run the student activity from the chapter: display two or three seal images and ask students to interpret the animal imagery — what animals are depicted, and why might a trader choose a particular animal to represent their goods or identity? Students write a short interpretation (three to four sentences) for one seal, justifying their reading. Two or three share with the class.

Consolidate: ask students to identify the three functions of Harappan seals — identifying goods, identifying traders, and linking to trade activities. Students add this to their trade-flow diagram from the previous unit, noting seals as a record-keeping and identification tool. This ties trade infrastructure back to the chapter's civilisation framework: writing (even if undeciphered) as a characteristic of civilisation.

periods.section_context: Overland, river, maritime trade routes, Lothal dockyard 217×36 metres, steatite seals, undeciphered script
periods.teacher_notes: This unit extends the trade analysis from craft production to the infrastructure and identification systems that made long-distance trade possible, drawing on the carnelian and bronze metallurgy evidence examined when the craft foundations of trade were introduced. A common confusion is treating Harappan seals as purely decorative; students should be guided to see them as functional trade and administrative tools, even though the script has not been deciphered. The undeciphered script is itself an important lesson about the limits of historical knowledge.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students analyse Harappan trade as an economic activity covering commodities, production techniques, routes, and infrastructure.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse how trade routes and physical infrastructure such as dockyards supported the reach and volume of an ancient civilisation's commercial network.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students interpret multiple source types — textual, archaeological, material — to construct historical understanding.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can interpret material artefacts such as seals and dockyard structures as evidence of economic organisation and administrative record-keeping.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students recognise and articulate India's civilisational contributions to human history including trade, technology, and urban planning.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify the Lothal dockyard and maritime trade network as evidence of India's early contribution to international commerce.

periods.activity_title: Everyday Objects: Reading Harappan Material Culture
materials: Projected or printed images of Harappan everyday objects: bronze mirrors, terracotta pots, stone weights, bronze chisel, carved stone gamesboard, terracotta whistle
periods.visual_aids: Image gallery of Harappan everyday objects: bronze mirror, terracotta pot, stone weights, bronze chisel, gamesboard, terracotta whistle

time_bands.activity: Display the six everyday objects one at a time: bronze mirror, terracotta pot, stone weights, bronze chisel, carved stone gamesboard, and terracotta whistle. For each object, ask one question: 'What was this used for?' After the class has named the function of each, ask: 'What do these six objects together tell us about daily life in a Harappan city?' Take four or five responses and write key ideas on the board.

Students work in groups of three. Each group selects two of the six objects and writes a short source analysis: (1) What is the object? (2) What material is it made from and what does that tell us about craft skill? (3) What aspect of Harappan life does it illuminate — practical work, commerce, leisure, or household activity? (4) What does this object NOT tell us about Harappan life that we would need another source to answer? Groups then share their analyses with the class.

Consolidate the object analyses by asking the class: 'The stone weights are all in precise ratios. What does the existence of standardised weights tell us about Harappan economic and administrative life?' Guide students to see that standard weights imply regulated trade and shared measurement conventions — a form of administration. Then ask: 'The gamesboard and whistle are not tools of work. What does their presence tell us?' Guide students to recognise that leisure and play are features of a society with enough surplus to allow time beyond bare survival.
Students write one sentence in their notebooks identifying which of the six objects they find the most revealing as a historical source, and explaining in one clause why.

periods.section_context: Bronze mirror, terracotta pots, stone weights, bronze chisel, gamesboard, terracotta whistle, craft and leisure
periods.teacher_notes: This unit develops students' ability to read everyday material objects as primary historical sources, building on the seal-interpretation work introduced when trade artefacts were examined. A common confusion is treating objects as self-evident — students often state what an object is without interrogating what it implies; the fourth analysis question ('what does this NOT tell us?') is designed to push beyond surface description. The standardised weights are particularly powerful evidence of economic administration and repay careful attention.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students interpret multiple source types — textual, archaeological, material — to construct historical understanding.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse everyday material objects as primary sources to infer aspects of craft skill, economic organisation, and daily life in an ancient civilisation.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students study early Indian civilisation as a case of settled urban life, covering agriculture, construction, metallurgy, water technology, craft, trade, and cultural life.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can use material evidence from everyday objects to characterise the craft production, economic activity, and leisure practices of a settled urban civilisation.

periods.activity_title: Symbols, Figurines, and Meanings: Reading Harappan Cultural Objects
materials: Projected or printed images of: Priest King statuette, swastika seal, three-faced deity seal, Dancing Girl figurine, namaste terracotta figurine, Lothal pot crow design
periods.visual_aids: Image gallery of Harappan cultural and symbolic objects: Priest King, swastika seal, three-faced deity seal, Dancing Girl (10.8 cm), namaste figurine, Lothal crow-story pot

time_bands.activity: Display the six cultural and symbolic objects: the 'Priest King' statuette, swastika seal, three-faced deity seal, Dancing Girl bronze figurine (10.8 cm, from Mohenjo-daro), namaste terracotta figurine, and the Lothal pot design that seems to depict the thirsty crow story. Ask students: 'How is this set of objects different from yesterday's set of everyday items?' Guide students to notice that this group seems to be about meaning, belief, identity, and story — not just practical function.

Work through each object with the class. For the Priest King: the name is a modern interpretation — ask students what the draped robe, closed eyes, and headband might suggest about the figure's status, and note that identity remains unknown. For the three-faced deity surrounded by animals: ask what it might suggest about Harappan beliefs. For the Dancing Girl: note its extraordinary technical skill in bronze casting, its small size (10.8 cm), and ask what it implies about artistic practice and celebration. For the Lothal pot: ask students to identify which familiar story it seems to depict and what this reveals about oral tradition.

Run the chapter's student activity: students examine the full set of cultural objects and identify which aspects of Harappan life seem most important to them. Students write a short paragraph (five to six sentences) making an argument: 'The most important aspect of Harappan cultural life visible in these objects is [X] because [evidence from two or more objects].' Two or three students share their paragraphs.

Consolidate by asking: 'What do these cultural objects tell us about Harappan civilisation that the drainage system and the Great Bath do not?' Guide students to recognise that material culture gives us access to belief, identity, and artistic expression — dimensions of civilisation the chapter's opening framework included as 'cultural ideas about life.' Students note this connection in their notebooks.

periods.section_context: Priest King, swastika seal, three-faced deity seal, Dancing Girl Mohenjo-daro, namaste figurine, Lothal pot
periods.teacher_notes: This unit uses symbolic and artistic objects to access Harappan belief and identity, extending the object-based source analysis developed when everyday objects were examined. A common confusion is treating the modern name 'Priest King' as established fact — students should understand that it is an interpretive label and the figure's identity is unknown; this is a good moment to reinforce that historians name things provisionally. The Lothal pot crow design is a natural bridge to cultural continuity, which will become explicit in the unit on the civilisation's end.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students interpret multiple source types — textual, archaeological, material — to construct historical understanding.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can interpret symbolic and artistic artefacts as evidence of belief systems, identity, and cultural expression in an ancient civilisation.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students identify elements of Harappan cultural life that show continuity with later Indian civilisation and contemporary practice.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify specific cultural symbols and gestures from Harappan artefacts that persist in later Indian civilisation and contemporary life.

periods.activity_title: Climate, Rivers, and Collapse: Why Did the Cities Empty?
periods.section_anchor: The End or a New Beginning?
materials: Timeline strip on the board (2600 BCE — peak urbanisation; 2200 BCE — global climate change begins; 1900 BCE — cities abandoned; dispersal to rural settlements)
periods.visual_aids: Timeline on board: 3500 BCE village growth → 2600 BCE full urbanisation → 2200 BCE climate change → 1900 BCE city abandonment

time_bands.activity: Draw the timeline on the board and walk students through it: cities at peak from 2600 BCE; global climatic change from about 2200 BCE causing reduced rainfall; drying of the Sarasvatī River in its central basin; cities such as Kalibangan and Banawali suddenly abandoned; by around 1900 BCE the urban phase is over. Ask: 'If you were a farmer in Kalibangan in 1950 BCE and the river near your city had dried up, what would you do?' Take responses to prime students for the causal analysis ahead.

Introduce the two currently accepted causes of decline: (1) global climatic change from around 2200 BCE that reduced rainfall and made agriculture more difficult; (2) the drying up of the Sarasvatī River in its central basin, which made the densely settled Sarasvatī corridor unsustainable. Note that early theories attributing the decline to warfare or invasion are now ruled out — there is no evidence of armies or weapons of war. Ask: 'What type of evidence would you need to find at a site to prove or disprove the warfare theory?' Guide students to think about what 'no evidence' means in archaeology.

Students construct a written cause-and-effect chain in their notebooks: beginning with 'global climate change from 2200 BCE' and ending with 'population disperses into small rural settlements.' They must include at least four steps, naming specific sites (Kalibangan, Banawali) and specific effects (reduced rainfall → harder agriculture → unsustainable cities → abandonment → dispersal). Pairs compare their chains and identify any steps they differ on.

Close by presenting the chapter's title for this section: 'The End or a New Beginning?' Ask: 'Which framing do you think is more accurate, and why?' Take two or three responses. Introduce the key point from the chapter: much Harappan culture and technology survived and was passed on to the next phase of Indian civilisation. Note that this idea of cultural survival will be examined more closely in the unit on continuity.

periods.section_context: 2200 BCE climate change, Sarasvatī drying, Kalibangan and Banawali abandoned, 1900 BCE dispersal, no warfare evidence
periods.teacher_notes: This unit traces the decline of the Sindhu-Sarasvatī civilisation as a societal transformation driven by environmental change, connecting the river geography introduced when the Sarasvatī's importance was first established. A common confusion is conflating the two causes — students may treat climate change and the drying of the Sarasvatī as the same event; they should be understood as related but distinct: a global climate shift reduced rainfall across a wide region, while the specific drying of the Sarasvatī had a locally concentrated impact on the densest cluster of Harappan settlements. The 'no evidence of warfare' point is important for teaching historical reasoning: absence of evidence is also meaningful data.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students explain major historical changes and their societal impact, including the transformation from villages to planned cities and the later decline.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct a multi-step causal explanation linking environmental change to the societal impact of civilisational decline.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students connect natural phenomena and river systems to human settlement patterns and civilisational development.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace how climatic change and river drying caused the abandonment of specific Harappan cities and dispersal of urban populations.

periods.activity_title: What Survived? Tracing Harappan Cultural Continuity into Later India
periods.section_anchor: The End or a New Beginning?
materials: Images of: contemporary bangles covering the arm (Gujarat/Rajasthan), namaste gesture, swastika symbol in use today
periods.visual_aids: Side-by-side image pairs: Harappan artefact and its contemporary counterpart (bangle style, namaste figurine and gesture, swastika seal and contemporary use)

time_bands.activity: Display the side-by-side image pairs. Ask students to identify what is the same and what is different in each pair. Introduce the chapter's key claim for this section: even though the cities were abandoned around 1900 BCE, much Harappan culture and technology survived and was passed on to the next phase of Indian civilisation. Ask: 'How can something survive if the cities are gone?' Guide students to think about people moving, taking knowledge, customs, and skills with them.

Work through each continuity example from the chapter: bangles covering an entire arm (still visible in Gujarat and Rajasthan); the namaste gesture (terracotta figurine in namaste pose); the swastika symbol (Harappan seal versus contemporary use); the Dancing Girl figurine as evidence of artistic tradition; and the Lothal pot crow design as evidence of oral story tradition. For each, ask students: 'Is this continuity, or could it be coincidence — the same idea arising independently?' This is a genuine historical question; both answers are defensible.

Students write a structured argument in their notebooks: 'I [agree / am not sure / disagree] that the items above show cultural continuity from Harappan times to today because [two pieces of evidence from the objects and chapter].' Students must take a position and support it with specific artefacts by name. Two or three students share their arguments; the class identifies where the evidence is strongest and where it is most ambiguous.

Consolidate: ask students why cultural continuity matters for how we think about Indian civilisation. Guide students to the idea that the Harappan civilisation is not a closed episode — it is a foundation. Students write one sentence: 'Harappan civilisation matters for India today because [reason].'

periods.section_context: Bangles in Gujarat-Rajasthan, namaste gesture, swastika symbol, Dancing Girl tradition, Lothal crow-story pot
periods.teacher_notes: This unit asks students to reason about cultural continuity as a historical claim that requires evidence, building on the cultural object analysis from the unit on symbolic artefacts. A common confusion is treating visual similarity as proof of continuity — students need to be challenged to distinguish between genuine transmission and independent parallel development; the structured argument task is designed to make this distinction explicit. The continuity question is also a direct answer to the chapter section's title 'The End or a New Beginning?' and students can now give a more evidence-based response to it.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students identify elements of Harappan cultural life that show continuity with later Indian civilisation and contemporary practice.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct an evidence-based argument about whether specific cultural practices show genuine continuity from an ancient civilisation into contemporary life.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students recognise and articulate India's civilisational contributions to human history including trade, technology, and urban planning.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify Harappan cultural innovations that persisted into later phases of Indian civilisation as evidence of a foundational civilisational legacy.

periods.activity_title: The Civilisation Framework Revisited: Applying Seven Criteria to the Harappans

time_bands.activity: Write the seven characteristics of civilisation on the board: government and administration, urbanism, variety of crafts, internal and external trade, writing, cultural ideas, productive agriculture. Ask students to recall what they now know about each one from the full body of Harappan evidence covered in the chapter. Take rapid oral responses for each characteristic — this is a retrieval warm-up, not an assessment.

Assign each group of three students two characteristics. Each group must produce a brief written case (four to five sentences) arguing that the Harappans fully met their two characteristics, drawing on at least two specific pieces of Harappan evidence per characteristic. Evidence must be specific and named: for example, 'the city-wide drainage network and Dholavira's six reservoirs show administration' or 'the undeciphered script on steatite seals shows some form of writing.' Groups write their cases in notebooks.

Each group presents their case to the class. After all seven characteristics have been presented, open a class discussion: 'Is there any characteristic where the Harappan evidence is weaker or more uncertain?' Guide students to notice that 'writing' is problematic — the script exists but cannot be read, so we cannot fully confirm its function. 'Government and administration' is inferred from infrastructure, not direct records. Discuss what this tells us about the limits of archaeological evidence.

Return to the Think About It question from the chapter's opening: 'Which characteristic is most fundamental?' Students compare their original claim (written in their notebooks in the first unit) with their current understanding. Ask two or three students whether they have changed their view and why. Students note their revised or confirmed position in one sentence.

periods.section_context: Seven civilisation characteristics tested against Harappan drainage, seals, agriculture, trade, crafts, urban planning
periods.teacher_notes: This unit returns to the chapter's opening framework to test it against the full body of Harappan evidence, closing a conceptual loop begun when the seven characteristics were first introduced. A common confusion at this stage is treating the framework as a checklist rather than an analytical tool — students should be pushed to think about degrees of evidence and gaps, not just yes/no ticks. The writing characteristic is the most productive source of genuine uncertainty and merits its own moment in the class discussion.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students study early Indian civilisation as a case of settled urban life, covering agriculture, construction, metallurgy, water technology, craft, trade, and cultural life.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can apply a multi-criteria framework to evaluate the extent to which an ancient civilisation meets each defining characteristic of complex settled society.

periods.activity_title: Urban Rise as Societal Change: Mapping the Village-to-City Transformation
materials: Timeline and map on board showing village growth from 3500 BCE, urbanisation by 2600 BCE, and key site locations
periods.visual_aids: Combined map-timeline: Indus-Sarasvatī region with site locations and arrow showing temporal progression from village settlement to urban network

time_bands.activity: Display the combined map-timeline. Ask students: 'What did a village in the Indus plains in 3500 BCE need to become a city by 2600 BCE?' List student responses on the board. Then introduce the chapter's framing of this transition as the 'First Urbanisation of India' — a fundamental societal change, not just population growth. Ask: 'What is the difference between a large village and a city?' Guide students toward the characteristics of planning, administration, specialisation, and infrastructure.

Students construct a comparison chart in their notebooks with two columns: 'Village (before 3500 BCE)' and 'City (by 2600 BCE).' They must fill each column using specific evidence from the chapter: for villages — smaller scale, agricultural base, rural supply function; for cities — wide cardinal-direction streets, fortifications, upper and lower towns, drainage systems, warehouses, dockyard (Lothal). After constructing the chart, students identify the three changes they consider most significant and rank them.

Open a class discussion: 'Was the transition from village to city a sudden change or a gradual one?' Guide students to use the chapter's evidence — villages growing from 3500 BCE, full urbanisation by 2600 BCE — to argue either way. Ask: 'What would have had to change in people's daily lives when a village became a city?' Push students beyond physical infrastructure to think about social changes: specialisation of labour, governance, contact with strangers.

Students write a two-sentence summary: 'The transformation from village to city between 3500 and 2600 BCE was significant because [reason 1]. The most important social change this brought was [reason 2].'

periods.section_context: 3500 BCE village growth, 2600 BCE full urbanisation, Harappa excavation, First Urbanisation of India
periods.teacher_notes: This unit deepens the societal change analysis of the village-to-city transition, going beyond geographical context to examine what changed in how people lived, worked, and were governed. A common confusion is treating urbanisation as simply 'more people' — the comparison chart is designed to push students toward qualitative social and administrative change. The discussion of gradual versus sudden change introduces students to how historians reason about pace of change.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students explain major historical changes and their societal impact, including the transformation from villages to planned cities and the later decline.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can compare the characteristics of village and urban life to explain the societal impact of the First Urbanisation of India.

periods.activity_title: Trade as Economy: Organising Harappan Commerce from Production to Exchange
materials: Blank trade-network diagram template (or students draw their own): nodes for production sites, trade routes, destination markets

time_bands.activity: Ask students: 'If you were a Harappan merchant in Lothal, what would you need to organise before you could send a shipment of carnelian beads and cotton to a distant trading partner?' Take responses. Then frame the unit's task: today students will build a complete picture of the Harappan trade economy — from raw material sourcing through production to distribution — as an integrated economic system, not just a list of goods.

Students construct a trade-network diagram in their notebooks. Nodes to include: carnelian source (Gujarat), conch shell source (coast), copper source (imported), cotton fields (river plains), craft workshops (bead drilling and shell-working), Lothal dockyard (maritime export), overland routes, and destination markets outside the civilisation. Students draw arrows showing the flow of raw materials into production and finished goods out to markets. They also note which goods were exported and which imported.

Pairs compare their diagrams and identify any differences. Then pose a class discussion question: 'The Harappans exported finished craft goods (carnelian beads, shell bangles) rather than raw materials. Why is this economically significant?' Guide students to see that processing raw materials adds value — a drilled and decorated carnelian bead is worth more than raw stone. Ask: 'What skills and organisation does this require?' Connect to craft specialisation, and to the chapter's civilisation framework: variety of crafts as a characteristic.

Consolidate by asking: 'Where do the steatite seals fit in this network?' Students add 'seals as identification and record-keeping tool' to their diagrams. Students write one sentence: 'The Harappan trade economy was distinctive because [reason drawn from their diagram].'

periods.section_context: Carnelian from Gujarat, shell bangles, Lothal dockyard, copper imports, cotton export, steatite seals system
periods.teacher_notes: This unit synthesises the trade evidence across the chapter into an integrated economic system diagram, building on the craft-production analysis from the carnelian and shell-bangle unit and the route and infrastructure analysis from the Lothal dockyard unit. A common confusion is treating imports and exports as symmetric — students should be pushed to notice that Harappans exported value-added finished goods while importing raw materials, which tells us something important about their craft capacity. The steatite seals as record-keeping tools connect trade back to the civilisation characteristic of writing.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students analyse Harappan trade as an economic activity covering commodities, production techniques, routes, and infrastructure.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct an integrated account of an ancient trade economy by tracing the flow of raw materials, craft production, and finished goods across a network of sites and routes.

periods.activity_title: India's First Gifts to the World: Identifying Harappan Civilisational Firsts

time_bands.activity: Ask students: 'What does it mean to say something was done for the first time by a particular civilisation?' Discuss briefly — it means no earlier evidence of that practice has been found anywhere else. Then ask students to generate from memory as many Harappan 'firsts' as they can. Collect answers on the board without evaluating yet.

Work through the chapter's documented firsts systematically: first intensive maritime activity in India (Lothal dockyard); first cotton cultivation in Eurasia; planned cities as among the earliest in the world; efficient water management including the Dholavira reservoir system; diverse crafts including carnelian bead drilling and bronze metallurgy; brisk trade networks spanning overland, river, and sea routes. For each, ask: 'Why does this matter beyond India — why is it a contribution to world history?' Take two or three responses per item.

Students write a structured reflective essay in their notebooks: 'The most significant contribution of the Sindhu-Sarasvatī civilisation to human history was [X]. I chose this because [two reasons using specific evidence from the chapter].' Students must choose one contribution, justify their choice with named evidence, and briefly acknowledge why a different choice could also be argued. They write for approximately ten minutes.

Three or four students share their essays. The class votes on which contribution was most compellingly argued (not necessarily most important), and the class articulates what made the chosen argument convincing — a specific detail, a clear reason, or a comparison to alternatives.

periods.section_context: First maritime activity India, first cotton cultivation Eurasia, planned cities, Dholavira water system, bronze metallurgy
periods.teacher_notes: This unit asks students to evaluate and prioritise the Harappan civilisation's contributions to world history, drawing on the full body of evidence accumulated across the chapter. A common confusion is listing contributions without distinguishing their significance — the essay task requires students to choose and justify, which forces the evaluative step. The class vote on the most compelling argument — rather than the 'correct' answer — is an important signal that historical significance is an argued claim, not a factual given.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students recognise and articulate India's civilisational contributions to human history including trade, technology, and urban planning.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate and prioritise the Harappan civilisation's contributions to world history by constructing a justified argument for the most significant contribution.

periods.activity_title: How Do We Know? Interrogating Archaeological Sources Across the Chapter
materials: List on board of source types mentioned in the chapter: excavated objects, bones, residue analysis, seals, architectural remains, textual sources (Rig Veda)

time_bands.activity: Write on the board: 'Claim: The Harappans traded in cotton.' Ask students: 'How do historians know this?' Take responses. Then introduce the unit's core question: every claim in this chapter rests on a particular type of source, and different source types have different strengths and limits. Display the list of source types on the board and ask students to add any they can think of from the chapter.

Students work in groups of three. Each group is assigned one source type from the list: (A) excavated objects and artefacts; (B) food residue and bone analysis; (C) architectural remains; (D) steatite seals; (E) textual sources (Rig Veda). Each group answers three questions in writing: (1) What specific claims in the chapter rest on this source type? (2) What can this source type tell us that others cannot? (3) What can this source type NOT tell us — where does it leave gaps? Groups record their answers in notebooks.

Groups report back. After each group, ask the class: 'Has any other group's source type filled the gap this group identified?' Build a class matrix on the board: source type in rows, strengths and gaps in columns. Discuss: 'The Harappan script on seals has not been deciphered. What does this gap mean for our understanding of Harappan administration and trade?' Push students to recognise that the undeciphered script is one of the most significant remaining limits on our knowledge.
Students write one sentence: 'The source type that gives us the most complete picture of Harappan life is [X] because [reason], but it cannot tell us [gap].'

periods.section_context: Excavated artefacts, bone and residue analysis, seals, architectural evidence, Rig Veda text, undeciphered script
periods.teacher_notes: This unit develops a meta-level understanding of how archaeological and textual sources work together and separately to reconstruct ancient civilisations, applying the source-type framework to the full range of evidence used in this chapter. A common confusion is treating 'more sources' as automatically meaning 'more certainty' — students should understand that different source types answer different questions, and some questions (particularly about Harappan administration and beliefs) remain genuinely open because the script has not been deciphered. The matrix built on the board is a useful summary tool for this unit's learning.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students interpret multiple source types — textual, archaeological, material — to construct historical understanding.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the strengths and limits of different archaeological and textual source types for constructing knowledge about an ancient civilisation.

periods.activity_title: Environment and Civilisation: Connecting Natural Systems to Human History
materials: Map showing Ghaggar-Hakra course and density of Harappan sites
periods.visual_aids: Map of Ghaggar-Hakra course with Harappan site density visible, alongside a second map showing the same region today

time_bands.activity: Display the map showing the density of Harappan sites along the Ghaggar-Hakra (ancient Sarasvatī) course. Ask students: 'What pattern do you notice about where the sites cluster?' Establish that the highest density of sites is along this river's course, including major cities Rakhigarhi and Ganweriwala and smaller settlements Farmana, Kalibangan, Bhirrana, and Banawali. Ask: 'What does this spatial pattern tell us about the relationship between this river and the civilisation?'

Now introduce the present-day reality: the Sarasvatī / Ghaggar-Hakra now flows only seasonally and has largely dried up. Ask students: 'If the river that supported this dense cluster of cities dried up, what would happen to those cities?' Then connect this to the chapter's climate change evidence: from around 2200 BCE, global climatic change reduced rainfall; the Sarasvatī dried up in its central basin; cities like Kalibangan and Banawali were suddenly abandoned. Ask students to trace the causal chain from environment to settlement to abandonment.

Students draw a cause-effect map in their notebooks with three zones: (1) natural event (river drying, rainfall reduction); (2) agricultural and economic consequences (harder farming, failed crops, reduced trade); (3) human response (city abandonment, dispersal to small rural settlements). They must name at least three specific sites in their map. After completing, pairs compare and identify where their maps differ.

Consolidate with a discussion question: 'Is the drying of the Sarasvatī a geographic event or a historical event?' Guide students to see that it is both — it is a natural phenomenon with a profound historical consequence. Ask: 'Can we find similar examples of natural changes shaping human history in other contexts?' Take one or two student suggestions. Students write one sentence connecting the Sarasvatī's drying to the civilisation's transformation.

periods.section_context: Sarasvatī basin site density, Ghaggar-Hakra seasonal flow, Rakhigarhi, Kalibangan abandonment, geographic-historical connection
periods.teacher_notes: This unit explores the intersection of geography and history through the Sarasvatī River as both a natural and a civilisational phenomenon, drawing on the river's role in settlement distribution established when the Sarasvatī section was first examined. A common confusion is treating the river's drying as a sudden catastrophe rather than a process — students should understand from the chapter's dates that the drying developed over decades and centuries, which is itself an important point about how environmental change works. The cause-effect map is designed to force students to think in chains rather than single causes.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students connect natural phenomena and river systems to human settlement patterns and civilisational development.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct a causal explanation connecting the drying of a river system to the spatial pattern of settlement abandonment and population dispersal.

periods.activity_title: Reading the Great Bath: Structured Debate on Archaeological Interpretation
materials: Image of the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro (projected or printed)
Two-column debate planning sheet (drawn in notebooks)
periods.visual_aids: Plan and photograph of the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro (12 × 7 metres, surrounding rooms, well)

time_bands.activity: Display the Great Bath image and review its features: a waterproofed tank measuring 12 × 7 metres in the upper town at Mohenjo-daro, surrounded by small rooms and served by a well. Remind students that two interpretations remain on the table: a royal bath used by city rulers, or a tank for religious rituals used by the broader community. Ask students to silently choose one interpretation before any discussion begins.

Run a structured debate. Divide the class into two groups regardless of personal preference. Group A argues: 'The Great Bath was a royal bath.' Group B argues: 'It was a religious ritual tank.' Each group has ten minutes to prepare their argument using only evidence from the chapter: location in the upper town, waterproofing technique, surrounding small rooms (changing rooms? priests' rooms?), connection to a well, central position in the city. Each group nominates one speaker to present their argument in two minutes.

After both presentations, open cross-examination: each group asks one question of the other group's evidence. The class then discusses: 'Is this a question that more archaeological evidence could resolve, or will it remain uncertain?' Ask: 'What physical evidence would you need to find in those surrounding small rooms to confirm the religious interpretation? What would confirm the royal interpretation?' Guide students to recognise that the answer depends on what kind of objects are found — religious items versus royal regalia.

Students write a verdict in their notebooks: 'Based on the evidence available, I think the Great Bath was [interpretation] because [two pieces of evidence]. However, this interpretation is [certain / uncertain] because [limitation of the evidence].'

periods.section_context: Great Bath Mohenjo-daro 12×7 metres, upper town, surrounding rooms, waterproofing, royal versus ritual interpretations
periods.teacher_notes: This unit uses the Great Bath as a case study in archaeological interpretation under uncertainty, applying the source-analysis and argumentation skills developed when the chapter's source types were interrogated across the civilisation. A common confusion is treating historical interpretation as a matter of choosing the 'right' answer — students need to understand that where physical evidence is limited, competing interpretations can both be valid if each is argued from evidence. The cross-examination step is key: it teaches students to test the other side's evidence, not just assert their own.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students interpret multiple source types — textual, archaeological, material — to construct historical understanding.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct and defend a historical interpretation from archaeological evidence while acknowledging the limits that make alternative interpretations viable.

periods.activity_title: Mapping the Civilisation: Geography, Extent, and the Obsolete Label
materials: Printed or projected map showing the full extent of the Sindhu-Sarasvatī civilisation: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi, Ganweriwala, Lothal, and smaller sites
periods.visual_aids: Map of the full extent of the Sindhu-Sarasvatī civilisation with all major and minor sites plotted and modern state/country boundaries overlaid

time_bands.activity: Display the full-extent map. Ask students to trace the westernmost and easternmost, northernmost and southernmost sites. Ask: 'Does this civilisation fit inside the Indus valley?' Establish that it extends well beyond — into Gujarat, Haryana, and across what is now Pakistan. Explain that this geographical reality is why the label 'Indus Valley civilisation' is now considered obsolete: the civilisation was much larger than the Indus valley alone.

Ask students to identify on the map: (1) which sites are in present-day Pakistan; (2) which are in present-day India, and in which states; (3) which sites are near the Indus River; (4) which are near the Ghaggar-Hakra (ancient Sarasvatī) course. Students annotate their own copy of the map or draw a sketch map in notebooks, marking these four categories with different symbols. After annotating, ask: 'What does the spread of sites suggest about the civilisation's reach and organisation?'

Pose a reasoning question: 'If you were a historian deciding what to name this civilisation, what name would you choose and why?' Students discuss in pairs for three minutes, then share with the class. Names from the chapter — Indus, Harappan, Indus-Sarasvatī, Sindhu-Sarasvatī — are compared. Ask: 'What does each name emphasise, and what does it leave out?' Guide students to see that naming is an interpretive act, not a neutral description.

Consolidate: ask students to identify one thing the map tells them about the civilisation that the text of the chapter does not convey as powerfully. Students write one sentence noting this observation. This consolidates map literacy as a distinct historical tool.

periods.section_context: Civilisation extent beyond Indus valley, Dholavira Gujarat, Rakhigarhi Haryana, obsolete Indus Valley label, naming as interpretation
periods.teacher_notes: This unit uses the civilisation's full geographical extent to teach both map literacy and the interpretive nature of historical naming, extending the geographical grounding established when the chapter first introduced the Indus-Sarasvatī region and the Punjab-Sindh plains. A common confusion is treating the label 'Harappan' as definitive — students should understand that it reflects the order of excavation, not the civilisation's centre of gravity. The naming discussion is genuinely open and invites authentic reasoning.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students study early Indian civilisation as a case of settled urban life, covering agriculture, construction, metallurgy, water technology, craft, trade, and cultural life.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can use a geographical map to reason about the spatial extent and territorial reach of an early urban civilisation.

periods.activity_title: Role Play — Governing a Harappan City: Decisions in an Urban Administration
materials: Role card set (teacher-prepared): City Planner, Water Engineer, Grain Warehouse Manager, Trade Overseer, Craft Workshop Supervisor

time_bands.activity: Distribute or assign role cards: City Planner, Water Engineer, Grain Warehouse Manager, Trade Overseer, and Craft Workshop Supervisor. Explain the scenario: the city of Dholavira is growing rapidly, a new residential area must be added, and the city's water supply — currently served by six reservoirs — needs to be extended. Each role-holder must advise what their domain requires from the new construction. Read out the role descriptions briefly.

Each student (or small group sharing a role) prepares a brief written advisory (four to five sentences) in character: what their role requires in the new residential area, and what will go wrong if their requirement is not met. Specific chapter evidence must be used: the Water Engineer must reference the underground drain connections and the reservoir scale; the City Planner must reference the cardinal-direction street grid and the upper-lower town division; the Trade Overseer must reference the need for warehouse space and seal-based record-keeping.

Each role presents their advisory to the 'city council' (the class). After all five advisories, the class must make two decisions: (1) Where in the new area will the drains go — under the streets, which means streets must be planned first? (2) Who has authority when two roles conflict (for example, the Water Engineer needs ground space for a new reservoir, but the Grain Warehouse Manager wants the same space)? Students vote on both decisions and give a reason.

Debrief out of character: 'What did this activity reveal about what kind of administration Harappan cities needed?' Students write one sentence noting the most important administrative insight the role play produced.

periods.section_context: Dholavira reservoirs, underground drains, city-wide drainage, warehouses, administration of urban infrastructure
periods.teacher_notes: This unit uses a structured role play to make visible the administrative coordination required to build and maintain Harappan urban infrastructure, building on the analytical work done when the Dholavira reservoir system and city-wide drainage were examined. A common confusion in role play is students speaking as individuals rather than as role-holders — remind them that each advisory must be grounded in specific chapter evidence, not general opinion. The conflict between roles (reservoir space versus warehouse space) is a designed feature: it mimics the genuine trade-offs city planners face and makes administration legible as decision-making under constraint.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students study early Indian civilisation as a case of settled urban life, covering agriculture, construction, metallurgy, water technology, craft, trade, and cultural life.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can demonstrate the administrative coordination required for complex urban infrastructure by reasoning through decision-making scenarios grounded in evidence from an early civilisation.

periods.activity_title: Harappan Trade in a World Economy: Connecting India to Distant Civilisations
materials: Map showing Harappan external trade connections to Mesopotamia and other regions beyond the subcontinent
periods.visual_aids: Map showing Harappan trade connections to regions outside the subcontinent, with trade route arrows and commodity labels

time_bands.activity: Display the external trade map. Explain that Harappan trade extended not only within the civilisation but also with distant cultures and civilisations inside and outside India. Ask students: 'What would a trader from Mesopotamia have wanted from the Harappans, and what would a Harappan merchant have wanted from Mesopotamia?' Take responses to activate prior knowledge about the trade commodity list.

Work through the chapter's external trade evidence: exports including ornaments, timber, objects of daily use, gold, cotton, and food items; imports including copper. Note that trade was conducted overland, along rivers, and by sea — the first intensive maritime activity in India. Ask: 'What does the existence of maritime trade routes to distant civilisations tell us about Harappan navigational and boat-building knowledge?' Guide students to infer from the evidence without overstating it.

Students write a structured analysis (five to six sentences) from the perspective of a historian making the case that the Harappan civilisation was 'globally connected' in its time: what evidence supports this claim? They must name at least three specific pieces of evidence (Lothal dockyard, maritime routes, copper imports, carnelian bead exports). periods.activity_title: The Decline Revisited: Evaluating Theories and Weighing Evidence
periods.section_anchor: The End or a New Beginning?
materials: Board summary of three theories of decline: (A) warfare/invasion (ruled out), (B) climate change (accepted), (C) river drying (accepted)

time_bands.activity: Write on the board three theories of Harappan decline: (A) warfare or invasion; (B) global climatic change from 2200 BCE causing reduced rainfall; (C) drying of the Sarasvatī River in its central basin. Ask students: 'What kind of evidence would a historian need to accept or reject each theory?' Take responses. Then explain that the chapter has already given us the answers: theory A is ruled out because there is no evidence of armies or weapons of war; theories B and C are currently accepted based on climate data and site abandonment patterns.

Students construct a written evaluation of all three theories in their notebooks, using an evidence-based format for each: (1) State the theory; (2) Name the evidence that supports or contradicts it; (3) State whether it is accepted, rejected, or uncertain based on current evidence. For theory A, they must explain what 'ruling out' means — absence of evidence for warfare is itself meaningful evidence. For theories B and C, they must name specific sites (Kalibangan, Banawali) and specific dates (2200 BCE, 1900 BCE).

Class discussion: 'Is the drying of the Sarasvatī River a cause of the decline or a symptom of the same climate change that caused the decline?' This is a genuinely complex question — both answers are defensible. Ask students to argue both positions in brief. Then ask: 'Does it matter which came first — the climate change or the river drying — for explaining why the cities collapsed?' Guide students to see that the distinction matters for understanding which factor was decisive.

Students write a two-sentence summary: 'The currently accepted explanation for the decline of the Sindhu-Sarasvatī civilisation is [explanation]. The evidence that most convinces me is [specific evidence and site].' This consolidates the unit's evaluative task.

periods.section_context: Decline theories: warfare ruled out, climate change 2200 BCE, Sarasvatī drying, Kalibangan Banawali abandoned 1900 BCE
periods.teacher_notes: This unit develops students' ability to evaluate competing historical theories by weighing evidence, extending the causal analysis of decline constructed in earlier work on the civilisation's end. A common confusion is treating the two accepted causes (climate change and river drying) as two separate explanations that need to be chosen between — students should understand they are mutually reinforcing, not mutually exclusive. The question of whether river drying is a cause or a symptom of climate change is genuinely unresolved and models how historical debate actually works.

periods.activity_title: The Whole Chapter in View: Connecting Rise, Flourishing, and Transformation of the Sindhu-Sarasvatī Civilisation
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for class timeline and concept web

time_bands.activity: Ask students to call out, from memory, every major phase or theme of the chapter. Record responses on the board in the order they are offered — do not organise them yet. Expected contributions: civilisation characteristics, village-to-city transition, Sarasvatī River, town-planning, water management, agriculture and food, trade and crafts, material culture, decline. After the list is complete, ask: 'What is the single story that connects all of these?'

Students construct a concept web in their notebooks. At the centre they write: 'Sindhu-Sarasvatī Civilisation (~3500–1900 BCE).' They then draw five to six branches, each labelled with one major theme from the board list, and add to each branch two or three specific pieces of evidence from the chapter — named artefacts, sites, dates, or technologies. After completing their own web, pairs share and add any items the other missed. Students may not invent connections — every branch must be traceable to a specific chapter section.

Run a whole-class synthesis discussion using three questions in sequence. First: 'Which feature of the Sindhu-Sarasvatī civilisation best demonstrates that it was a civilisation and not merely a collection of villages — and why?' Second: 'The civilisation declined around 1900 BCE. Did it truly end, or did something survive — and what is the evidence?' Third: 'What is the single most important thing the Sindhu-Sarasvatī civilisation contributed to the story of India?' Students contribute from their webs; the teacher records key claims on the board under each question.

Students write a three-sentence synthesis statement in their notebooks: sentence one names the civilisation's most distinctive feature and the evidence for it; sentence two names the cause of its transformation; sentence three names its legacy for Indian civilisation. This is their own closing statement on the chapter, and there is no single correct answer — it must be argued from evidence.

assessment_items.question_text: A student lists four features observed at an ancient site: (i) houses with drainage channels connected to a street-level system; (ii) farmers growing grain in nearby fields; (iii) small steatite objects bearing animal figures and script signs used to mark goods; (iv) bronze tools made from a combination of copper and tin. options.label: A
options.text: They indicate the people practised farming, which is the defining feature that distinguishes civilisation from nomadic life.

options.label: B
options.text: They prove the settlement had a written language, which is the single most important feature that separates civilisations from villages.

options.label: C

options.label: D

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reduces the civilisation-village distinction to agriculture alone, ignoring that villages also practise farming; misses the combinatory logic of the seven-characteristic framework.
