assessment_items.task: Create a cause-effect map that shows how the Dholavira water management system — its six large reservoirs, underground drains, and city-wide distribution network — required administrative planning before and during construction. Your map must show: (i) what had to be decided before any building began; (ii) what would break down if one part of the system was not coordinated with the others; (iii) what the system's existence tells us about the kind of governance Dholavira had.
assessment_items.scaffold: Start by writing 'Dholavira: Decision to Build Water System' in a box at the top. Draw arrows downward showing what decisions had to come first (street layout? reservoir locations? drain routes?). Then draw a second layer showing what each decision depended on — if streets were not planned first, what could not be built? Add a third layer: what would a farmer, a city official, and a craft worker each need from this system? At the bottom, write one sentence: 'This system tells us Dholavira had [type of governance] because [reason from the map].'
format_of_output: A hand-drawn cause-effect map with labelled boxes and arrows, completing all three layers described in the scaffold
One concluding sentence about governance written below the map
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may produce a written list organised under three headings matching the three layers, or complete the task verbally with a partner while the teacher circulates.

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The task requires students to reason about administrative sequencing — not just identify that a system existed, but explain why its complexity implies coordinated governance. This directly demonstrates the LO's demand: evaluating infrastructure as evidence of administrative and engineering capacity.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The three-layer scaffold moves students from pre-construction decisions (layer 1) to systemic interdependence (layer 2) to governance inference (layer 3). A student who completes all three layers with named evidence (reservoirs, drains, city-wide distribution) has met the full demand. A student who only completes layer 1 has demonstrated understanding but not evaluation.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: names specific features of the Dholavira system (six reservoirs, underground drains, 73-metre largest reservoir); shows genuine causal sequencing (streets must precede drains; reservoir locations must precede drain routing); governance inference is specific ('coordinating labour across multiple construction phases implies a central authority'). Weak: lists features without causal arrows; governance inference is vague ('they must have had a government'); no specific Dholavira evidence named.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A cause-effect map is the most natural demonstration vehicle because the LO requires students to trace chains of administrative dependency — not just describe outcomes but show how each decision caused or constrained the next. A written paragraph would not make the sequencing and interdependence visible in the same way. The teacher may substitute any other format from the Open Task menu that makes causal sequencing visible.

An archaeological map of the same region shows the highest concentration of Harappan sites clustered along the Ghaggar-Hakra course. Which conclusion can be drawn ONLY by using both sources together — a conclusion that neither source alone could support?

options.label: A
options.text: The Sarasvatī River was both a culturally revered river and the geographical backbone of the densest cluster of Harappan settlement, suggesting it sustained the civilisation at its core.

options.label: B
options.text: The Rig Veda is a reliable historical document because it accurately describes the geography of the Harappan period.

options.label: C
options.text: Harappan sites were built near rivers because people have always preferred to live near water, regardless of any particular civilisation.

options.label: D
options.text: The Sarasvatī River dried up because the Harappans used too much of its water for their cities and reservoirs.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Conflates using a text as evidence with validating it as wholly reliable — treats the combination of sources as a verification exercise rather than an inference-building exercise; misses the distinction between what a source tells us and what it proves.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Overgeneralises from the specific Sarasvatī evidence to a universal claim about human settlement — discards the particular historical content and replaces it with a truism that neither source is needed to establish.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces a causal claim not supported by either source — the chapter attributes river drying to global climate change, not human overuse; conflates the fact of settlement density with a theory of causation.

competency.competency_text: Students interpret multiple source types — textual, archaeological, material — to construct historical understanding.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the strengths and limits of different archaeological and textual source types for constructing knowledge about an ancient civilisation.
assessment_items.question_text: A student says: 'We know a lot about the Harappans because we have found thousands of seals with script on them.' A second student replies: 'Those seals actually show one of the biggest limits of our knowledge.' Which student is making the stronger argument, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Both students are equally right, because the seals give us some knowledge and limit other knowledge at the same time.

options.label: B
options.text: Neither student is correct, because seals are decorative objects and were not used to record information.

options.label: C
options.text: The first student is stronger, because a large number of seals means a large body of evidence, and more evidence always means more knowledge.

options.label: D
options.text: The second student is stronger, because although the seals prove a writing system existed, the script has not been deciphered — so the seals cannot tell us what the Harappans recorded, how they governed, or what they believed.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Treats quantity of evidence as equivalent to quality of knowledge — misses the critical point that undeciphered evidence cannot answer the questions historians most want answered; confuses presence of sources with accessibility of their content.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Attempts a balanced answer but avoids the evaluative judgment the question requires — 'both are equally right' is a deflection from the specific weakness the second student identifies; the two claims are not symmetrically valid.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Contradicts the chapter's explicit account of seals as trade and administrative identification tools — a recall error about the function of Harappan seals.

competency.competency_text: Students interpret multiple source types — textual, archaeological, material — to construct historical understanding.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct and defend a historical interpretation from archaeological evidence while acknowledging the limits that make alternative interpretations viable.
assessment_items.question_text: The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro is a waterproofed tank measuring 12 × 7 metres, located in the upper town, surrounded by small rooms, and connected to a well. Two interpretations exist: (i) it was a royal bath used by city rulers; (ii) it was a tank for religious rituals. Choose one interpretation and write a response that: (a) names two features of the Great Bath that support your chosen interpretation, and (b) names one feature that the other interpretation could also use as evidence, explaining why this means your conclusion is uncertain.
expected_elements: Clearly states which interpretation is being argued.

Names two specific features of the Great Bath (from: waterproofed tank, upper-town location, surrounding small rooms, connection to a well, 12 × 7 metres size) and explains how each supports the chosen interpretation.
Names one feature that the opposing interpretation could also claim as evidence — and explains specifically why it does not definitively rule out that interpretation.
Acknowledges that the conclusion is uncertain rather than established as fact.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may respond in point form rather than prose if they find structuring a paragraph difficult; the teacher may pair students for verbal rehearsal before individual written response.

expected_elements: Clearly states which interpretation is being argued.
Names two specific features of the Great Bath and explains how each supports the chosen interpretation.
Names one feature that the opposing interpretation could also claim as evidence and explains why it does not definitively settle the question.
Acknowledges that the conclusion is uncertain rather than established as fact.

competency.competency_text: Students explain major historical changes and their societal impact, including the transformation from villages to planned cities and the later decline.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare the characteristics of village and urban life to explain the societal impact of the First Urbanisation of India.
assessment_items.question_text: Between roughly 3500 BCE and 2600 BCE, settlements in the Indus-Sarasvatī plains transformed from villages into the cities of the First Urbanisation of India. Which of the following best describes a societal change — not just a physical change — that this transformation would have required?

options.label: A
options.text: People would have had to build larger houses, because the defining difference between a village and a city is the size of individual dwellings.

options.label: B
options.text: People would have had to develop new forms of coordinated decision-making and specialised roles — such as planners, warehouse managers, and craft specialists — because a city cannot function with each household acting independently.

options.label: C
options.text: People would have had to move closer to rivers, because cities need more water than villages and rivers were the only available water source.

options.label: D
options.text: People would have needed to start farming, because cities cannot survive without agricultural production that did not exist in villages.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses a physical characteristic (proximity to water) with a societal change, and overstates the claim — villages also relied on rivers for water; the specific infrastructure change (wells, reservoirs) is more precise than simply 'moving closer.'
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reverses the chapter's evidence — the chapter establishes that agricultural villages already existed before urbanisation; cities were supplied by these villages, not the reverse.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reduces the village-to-city distinction to a physical scale measure (house size) and misses the chapter's emphasis on planning, administration, and specialisation as the defining societal differences.

competency.competency_text: Students explain major historical changes and their societal impact, including the transformation from villages to planned cities and the later decline.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate competing theories of historical decline by weighing the evidence for and against each and articulating the grounds for current scholarly consensus.
assessment_items.chapter_section: The End or a New Beginning?
assessment_items.question_text: Early scholars proposed that the Sindhu-Sarasvatī civilisation declined because of warfare or invasion. This theory is now ruled out. Which of the following best explains why historians rejected it?

options.label: A
options.text: No evidence of armies, weapons of war, or battle damage has been found at Harappan sites — and absence of this specific type of evidence is itself meaningful when a civilisation-wide pattern of peaceful archaeology is consistent.

options.label: B
options.text: The warfare theory was rejected because historians now prefer environmental explanations over military ones as a general rule.

options.label: C
options.text: The warfare theory was rejected because no foreign civilisation was powerful enough to defeat the Harappans at that time.

options.label: D
options.text: The warfare theory was rejected because the Harappans were known to be a peaceful people who never engaged in conflict.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Substitutes a methodological preference for an evidence-based reason — implies historians choose theories by disciplinary bias rather than by evaluating evidence; misrepresents how historical consensus forms.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Treats the conclusion (no warfare) as a prior known fact about Harappan character rather than an inference from the absence of evidence — circular reasoning that bypasses the evidential argument.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces a claim about external civilisations' power that is not supported by the chapter — imports a different historical argument and ignores the internal archaeological evidence that actually grounds the rejection.

competency.competency_text: Students explain major historical changes and their societal impact, including the transformation from villages to planned cities and the later decline.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct a multi-step causal explanation linking environmental change to the societal impact of civilisational decline.
assessment_items.chapter_section: The End or a New Beginning?
assessment_items.question_text: Write a four-step causal chain that explains the decline of the Sindhu-Sarasvatī civilisation from the global climate change of around 2200 BCE to the dispersal of the population by around 1900 BCE. Each step must name at least one specific site, date, or event from the chapter.
expected_elements: Step 1 names the global climatic change from around 2200 BCE and its direct environmental consequence — reduced rainfall.
Step 2 connects reduced rainfall to the drying of the Sarasvatī River in its central basin.
Step 3 names the specific effect on cities — cities such as Kalibangan and Banawali were suddenly abandoned as the river-dependent agricultural and water base collapsed.
Step 4 describes the societal outcome — the urban population dispersed into hundreds of small rural settlements with no evidence of the earlier government or administration.
Each step is causally connected to the next — the chain reads as a sequence, not a list.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who find linear prose difficult may present the chain as a numbered list with one sentence per step, or use arrows to connect labelled boxes in a diagram.

expected_elements: Step 1 names global climatic change from around 2200 BCE and reduced rainfall.
Step 2 connects reduced rainfall to the drying of the Sarasvatī River in its central basin.
Step 3 names specific abandoned cities — Kalibangan and/or Banawali — and the date of around 1900 BCE.
Step 4 describes dispersal into small rural settlements and loss of administration.
Each step is causally connected to the next, not simply listed.

competency.competency_text: Students analyse Harappan trade as an economic activity covering commodities, production techniques, routes, and infrastructure.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how craft specialisation and raw material sourcing formed the productive basis of an ancient civilisation's export trade.
assessment_items.question_text: Carnelian beads were among the most prized Harappan trade items. Carnelian is a reddish semiprecious stone found mainly in Gujarat. Harappan craftspeople developed special drilling and decorating techniques to work with it. Which of the following best explains why Harappan carnelian beads had high trade value?

options.label: A
options.text: Their value came entirely from the rarity of carnelian stone, because any trader who obtained the raw material could produce equally valuable beads.

options.label: B
options.text: Their value came from being made of metal, which was the most prized material in ancient trade networks.

options.label: C
options.text: Their value came from being used as currency, replacing the need for weighing and measuring goods in trade transactions.

options.label: D
options.text: Their value came from both the rarity of the raw material — sourced from a specific region — and the skill required to drill and decorate it, making the finished bead something that could not easily be produced elsewhere.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Understands that raw material sourcing contributes to value but ignores the craft specialisation dimension — treats the two value components as separable when the chapter presents them as jointly necessary.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Misidentifies the material — carnelian is a semiprecious stone, not a metal; this is a confusion between the carnelian bead trade and the chapter's separate discussion of bronze metallurgy.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Attributes a currency function to beads not supported by the chapter — confuses the use of standardised stone weights (the actual weighing and measuring tool) with the bead as a trade commodity.

competency.competency_text: Students analyse Harappan trade as an economic activity covering commodities, production techniques, routes, and infrastructure.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can analyse how trade routes and physical infrastructure such as dockyards supported the reach and volume of an ancient civilisation's commercial network.
assessment_items.question_text: The Lothal dockyard measured 217 × 36 metres. Harappans also traded overland and along rivers. Why is the existence of the Lothal dockyard particularly significant as evidence of Harappan trade?

options.label: A
options.text: It indicates that the Harappans invented the boat, since no earlier evidence of seafaring exists anywhere in the world.

options.label: B
options.text: It proves that Lothal was the largest and most important city in the Harappan civilisation.

options.label: C
options.text: It provides physical evidence that the Harappans conducted the first intensive maritime activity in India, enabling trade with distant partners that land and river routes alone could not reach at that scale.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows that sea trade was the only form of Harappan trade, making overland and river routes unnecessary.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Overstates the significance of the dockyard by treating it as exclusive evidence against other trade routes — the chapter explicitly names all three (overland, river, maritime) as part of the Harappan trade network.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Conflates the significance of Lothal's dockyard infrastructure with a claim about Lothal's overall urban importance — the chapter does not rank Lothal as the most important city; this is an unwarranted inference from size.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Overstates the claim — the chapter describes Lothal as evidence of 'the first intensive maritime activity in India,' not the invention of seafaring globally; this is an overbroad generalisation from a specific and geographically bounded claim.

competency.competency_text: Students analyse Harappan trade as an economic activity covering commodities, production techniques, routes, and infrastructure.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct an integrated account of an ancient trade economy by tracing the flow of raw materials, craft production, and finished goods across a network of sites and routes.
assessment_items.question_text: Harappans exported finished craft goods rather than raw materials. Using the example of carnelian beads, explain in three steps: (i) where the raw material came from and why its location mattered; (ii) what had to happen to the raw material before it could be traded; (iii) why exporting the finished bead rather than the raw stone was economically significant. Name at least one specific location or technique in your response.
expected_elements: Step (i) names Gujarat as the source of carnelian and notes that its specific geographical location meant the stone had to be transported before it could be worked.
Step (ii) describes the craft process — Harappan craftspeople applied special drilling and decorating techniques to transform the raw stone into a finished bead.
Step (iii) explains that a finished, decorated bead commanded higher trade value than raw stone because the craftsmanship added value that required specialised skill not easily replicated elsewhere.
At least one specific location (Gujarat) or technique (drilling, decorating) is named.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may draw a simple three-box flow diagram with labels as a substitute for prose paragraphs.

expected_elements: Step (i) names Gujarat as the carnelian source and notes the significance of the specific location.
Step (ii) describes the drilling and decorating craft process applied to the raw stone.
Step (iii) explains that the finished bead's value derives from added craft skill — exporting it retains that value rather than giving it to the buyer of raw stone.
At least one specific location or technique is named.

competency.competency_text: Students connect natural phenomena and river systems to human settlement patterns and civilisational development.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use spatial distribution of archaeological sites to reason about a river system's role in supporting human settlement.
assessment_items.question_text: Archaeological maps show the highest concentration of Harappan sites — including major cities Rakhigarhi and Ganweriwala, and smaller settlements Farmana, Kalibangan, Bhirrana, and Banawali — clustered along the Ghaggar-Hakra (ancient Sarasvatī) course. What can a historian reasonably infer from this spatial pattern alone?

options.label: A
options.text: Settlements along the Sarasvatī were all more important than those along the Indus River, because density of sites proves relative importance.

options.label: B
options.text: The map proves that the Rig Veda's description of the Sarasvatī as a great river is historically accurate in every detail.

options.label: C
options.text: The Sarasvatī River was a critical resource for the civilisation — the density of settlements along its course indicates that communities depended on it for water, fertile soil, and possibly transport.

options.label: D
options.text: The Sarasvatī was the only river in the region, so all settlements had no choice but to locate along it.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Factually incorrect and overstated — the chapter names the Indus River and its tributaries as additional river systems; this option ignores the broader geography of the civilisation.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Misreads density as a proxy for importance — the chapter does not rank Sarasvatī sites above Indus sites; this is an unwarranted inference from the map pattern.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Overextends from map evidence to textual validation — the map can tell us about settlement distribution but cannot confirm every detail of the Rig Veda's description; this conflates two separate source types and their different evidential scope.

competency.competency_text: Students connect natural phenomena and river systems to human settlement patterns and civilisational development.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct a causal explanation connecting the drying of a river system to the spatial pattern of settlement abandonment and population dispersal.
assessment_items.question_text: The Sarasvatī River dried up in its central basin during a period of global climatic change. Cities like Kalibangan and Banawali, located along its course, were suddenly abandoned around 1900 BCE. Which of the following best explains the causal connection between the river drying and the city abandonments?

options.label: A
options.text: City abandonments happened because the population chose to move to the Indus valley to found new cities there, following the river's disappearance.

options.label: B
options.text: The drying of the Sarasvatī caused the Indus River to dry up as well, which simultaneously destroyed all Harappan cities across the entire civilisation.

options.label: C
options.text: The river drying caused immediate flooding elsewhere, which forced people out of their cities and into surrounding areas.

options.label: D
options.text: When the river dried, it removed the water supply and fertile soil that agriculture depended on — without these, cities in the Sarasvatī basin could not feed themselves or sustain trade, making continued urban life impossible.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces a mechanism (flooding caused by drying) that contradicts the chapter's account — river drying reduces water, it does not produce floods in other areas; this is a physical geography error overlaid onto the historical explanation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Overgeneralises the Sarasvatī's drying to all rivers and all sites — the chapter is specific that the Sarasvatī dried in its central basin and that cities along it were abandoned; Indus-area sites followed a different trajectory.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Attributes an active, organised relocation decision to the dispersing population — the chapter describes dispersal into 'hundreds of small rural settlements,' not a coordinated founding of new cities; this misreads the societal impact of the decline.

competency.competency_text: Students connect the distribution of resources and geographical conditions to the development of differential infrastructure and technology across sites.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how geographical variation in available resources shaped differential water infrastructure across Harappan cities.
assessment_items.question_text: Mohenjo-daro used hundreds of brick-lined wells for its water supply. Dholavira, located in a different geographical setting, built at least six large stone-cut reservoirs connected by underground drains. What does the difference in these two water systems most likely reflect?

options.label: A
options.text: Dholavira had a larger population than Mohenjo-daro, and population size determined which water technology was chosen.

options.label: B
options.text: Dholavira was a more advanced civilisation than Mohenjo-daro, because reservoirs are always a more sophisticated technology than wells.

options.label: C
options.text: Mohenjo-daro had less administrative capacity than Dholavira, which is why it could only build individual wells rather than a coordinated reservoir system.

options.label: D
options.text: The different geographical settings of the two cities — Dholavira's access to rock suitable for cutting allowed reservoir construction, while Mohenjo-daro's setting was better suited to individual wells.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Ranks the two technologies in a linear hierarchy of sophistication — misses the chapter's point that both are appropriate solutions for different geographical conditions; treats complexity as inherently superior rather than context-dependent.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Attributes the well-based system to administrative weakness rather than environmental context — directly contradicts the chapter, which presents Mohenjo-daro's hundreds of wells as evidence of substantial planning and administration.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Introduces population size as the governing variable — the chapter does not provide comparative population figures and attributes the infrastructure difference to geography, not demography.

competency.competency_text: Students connect the distribution of resources and geographical conditions to the development of differential infrastructure and technology across sites.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace how the geographical distribution of raw materials such as carnelian and copper shaped the commodity structure of Harappan trade.
assessment_items.question_text: Carnelian, the raw material for some of the Harappans' most valued export goods, was found mainly in Gujarat. Copper, needed for the bronze tools and figurines the Harappans produced, was likely imported. What does the geographical distribution of these two materials tell us about the Harappan economy?

options.label: A
options.text: Because carnelian was found in Gujarat, most of the population lived in Gujarat to be near the raw material.

options.label: B
options.text: The geographical distribution of materials shows that Harappan cities were each self-sufficient and did not need to trade with one another.

options.label: C
options.text: The Harappans stopped using copper once they discovered carnelian, because semiprecious stones were more valuable than metals.

options.label: D
options.text: The uneven distribution of raw materials meant the Harappans depended on trade — not just to sell finished goods, but also to acquire essential materials they could not source within their own territory.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Conflates the location of a raw material with the location of the population — ignores the trade mechanism that moved carnelian from Gujarat to craft workshops elsewhere in the civilisation.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Fabricates a substitution relationship between carnelian and copper that the chapter does not support — both materials were used simultaneously for different purposes (ornaments versus tools and figurines).
what_each_option_reveals.B: Inverts the chapter's conclusion — the uneven geographical distribution of materials is precisely what made inter-city and external trade necessary; self-sufficiency is contradicted by the copper import evidence.

competency.competency_text: Students identify elements of Harappan cultural life that show continuity with later Indian civilisation and contemporary practice.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify specific cultural symbols and gestures from Harappan artefacts that persist in later Indian civilisation and contemporary life.
assessment_items.question_text: Among the cultural objects found at Harappan sites are: a terracotta figurine in a namaste pose, a seal bearing a swastika symbol, and shell bangles covering an entire arm — a style still visible in Gujarat and Rajasthan today. What does the presence of these objects at Harappan sites suggest about Indian cultural history?

options.label: A
options.text: Because the namaste gesture appears in a Harappan figurine, it was invented by the Harappans and could not have developed independently elsewhere.

options.label: B
options.text: Certain cultural practices and symbols that appear in the Harappan record — the namaste gesture, the swastika symbol, and specific bangle styles — are also visible in later Indian life, suggesting these elements may have persisted across a very long period.

options.label: C
options.text: Indian culture has not changed at all since the Harappan period, because the presence of the same objects proves complete cultural continuity.

options.label: D
options.text: The objects prove that Harappans and people in present-day Gujarat and Rajasthan are direct descendants sharing an unbroken genetic and cultural line.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Overstates the continuity evidence — 'the same objects' appearing across time does not prove 'complete cultural continuity'; this conflates partial similarity with total cultural stasis, ignoring the many changes that also occurred.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Moves from cultural evidence to a genetic claim that the archaeological record cannot support — conflates cultural similarity with biological descent, which requires different and much stronger evidence.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Treats Harappan origin as exclusive origin — ignores the possibility of independent parallel development, which the chapter itself acknowledges as a genuine interpretive question.

competency.competency_text: Students identify elements of Harappan cultural life that show continuity with later Indian civilisation and contemporary practice.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct an evidence-based argument about whether specific cultural practices show genuine continuity from an ancient civilisation into contemporary life.
assessment_items.chapter_section: The End or a New Beginning?
assessment_items.question_text: A student argues: 'The Harappan civilisation did not truly end — it transformed.' Which of the following best evaluates this claim using evidence from the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: The claim is not supported: the cities were abandoned and the government disappeared, so the civilisation ended completely with no continuity.

options.label: B
options.text: The claim is not verifiable because all Harappan cultural objects are unique and have no parallels in later Indian art or practice.

options.label: C
options.text: The claim is supported only if the Harappan script is deciphered, because cultural continuity cannot be claimed without written records.

options.label: D
options.text: The claim is well-supported: cultural practices such as the namaste gesture, bangle styles, and the swastika symbol appear in Harappan artefacts and remain visible in Indian life, and the chapter explicitly states that Harappan culture and technology were passed on to the next phase of Indian civilisation.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Conflates political and administrative collapse with total cultural extinction — acknowledges that the urban phase ended but ignores the chapter's explicit statement about cultural survival and transmission.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Factually contradicts the chapter — the chapter gives specific examples of Harappan cultural elements (namaste figurine, swastika seal, bangle styles) that have parallels in later Indian practice; 'no parallels' is demonstrably wrong.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Treats written records as a necessary condition for all historical claims — the chapter's argument for cultural continuity rests on material artefacts and explicit textual statement from the chapter summary, not on deciphering the script.

competency.competency_text: Students recognise and articulate India's civilisational contributions to human history including trade, technology, and urban planning.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify the Lothal dockyard and maritime trade network as evidence of India's early contribution to international commerce.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes Harappan maritime trade as 'the first intensive maritime activity in India.' The Lothal dockyard measured 217 × 36 metres. Which of the following best states why this maritime activity is historically significant for India?

options.label: A
options.text: It shows that Lothal was the capital city of the Harappan civilisation, because the capital would naturally control maritime trade.

options.label: B
options.text: It shows that sea trade was more important than land trade in the ancient world, making the Lothal dockyard the most significant Harappan contribution.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows that the earliest phase of Indian civilisation included large-scale organised sea trade, establishing India's participation in international commerce thousands of years ago.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows that the Harappans were the first people in the entire world to build ships, before any other civilisation discovered sea travel.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Overstates the chapter's claim globally — the chapter says 'first intensive maritime activity in India,' not first in the world; this is an over-generalisation of a geographically specific historical claim.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Creates a ranking between trade modes that the chapter does not support — the chapter presents overland, river, and maritime trade as complementary, not competing; and does not identify maritime as the 'most significant' contribution.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Infers political status from economic function — the chapter does not identify Lothal as a capital city; this is an unwarranted inference from the dockyard's scale.

competency.competency_text: Students recognise and articulate India's civilisational contributions to human history including trade, technology, and urban planning.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate and prioritise the Harappan civilisation's contributions to world history by constructing a justified argument for the most significant contribution.
assessment_items.question_text: A student is asked to identify the most significant Harappan contribution to world history and chooses 'first cotton cultivation in Eurasia.' A second student chooses 'planned cities with cardinal-direction street grids.' Which of the following best evaluates these two choices?

options.label: A
options.text: Both choices can be argued as significant, because cotton cultivation introduced a new crop and textile source to an entire continent, while planned urban grids established a model of organised city-building — the stronger argument depends on which criterion of significance is applied.

options.label: B
options.text: Cotton cultivation is definitely the more significant contribution because food and clothing are always more important than urban planning.

options.label: C
options.text: Neither contribution is significant because both have been replicated by other civilisations and are therefore not unique to the Harappans.

options.label: D
options.text: Planned cities are definitely more significant because architecture is the only contribution that survives physically and can be seen today.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Applies a fixed universal hierarchy of significance — treats 'food and clothing' as categorically more important than urban planning without justification; reduces a comparative evaluative question to a predetermined ranking.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces a criterion (physical survival) not relevant to historical significance — 'can be seen today' is a claim about archaeological preservation, not a measure of historical importance; also factually understates the survival of cotton's impact.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Treats 'first occurrence' as the only valid criterion for significance — ignores that the Harappan civilisation's documented status as the first in Eurasia to cultivate cotton and build planned cities is itself the basis of historical significance, regardless of later replication.
